ui.status: SCORE 7.90 IS STALE AND NO LONGER DESCRIBES THIS MODULE — it was awarded before the HUD skin and the item thumbnails landed on 2026-09-09, which rewrote hud.tsx, panel-host.tsx, parts.tsx, surface.ts and every panel body. Re-grade before quoting it. --- built, ungated. 4,629 lines across `lib/game/ui/` plus `lib/game/i18n/` (289 keys x en/de, up from 117), 22 selftest checks. THE MODULE IS A REGISTRY, NOT A SET OF HARD-WIRED PANELS: `registerPanel`, `registerInspector` (per entity kind) and `registerStat` (a figure in the top bar), each returning its own unregister, and the TEN built-in panels (park, rides, shops, guests, weather, inspector, log, saves, settings, help) plus two inspectors are registered through those exact calls — there is no privileged path, which is the only way the extensibility axis is actually tested. `Body` is a component rather than a render function so a foreign panel's hooks are its own. No wait time is displayed anywhere, because the sim computes one and does not publish it and a queue divided by a rated throughput is a different quantity wearing the same name; the ride inspector says so in both languages. Measured, with the caveat the critic added and the module had not: 4.78 React commits per publish with nothing open and 5.67 with three panels — but n is NINE publishes on each side, so the two decimals rest on nothing, and the ratio does not transfer to a real browser at all, because the publish is driven from `onRender`: a slow renderer lengthens the interval, more figures have moved when one lands, and more components therefore commit. Under SwiftShader a publish covers seconds of wall clock, at 60 fps it covers 250 ms. What DOES transfer is the model rather than the number — chrome about 4 commits per publish, plus exactly one per open panel that calls `useTelemetrySnapshot`, which is a structural claim anybody can check by reading which panels use the whole snapshot; 220 DOM nodes as chrome alone, 538 with three panels; zero draw calls and zero triangles, because it is DOM over the canvas. Verified at 1920x1080, 1280x720 in German and 390x844 across five times of day; the phone layout was measured rather than guessed — the desktop arrangement needs 396 px of chrome in 378 px, so the rows split, the rail wraps instead of scrolling and the panel sheet sits above the build bar. It also caught the `sim:timeout` notice lying: 'The simulation did not start' stood 800 px from a panel reporting 1,441 guests and 4/4 rides running, and it now retracts itself when a frame arrives while the entry stays in the messages panel. Weakest: no worker query channel, which is eight of its ten listed weaknesses seen from different panels. GRADED 7.9, FAIL. No hard gate broken and the budget met with room; what holds it under the bar is that four of the twelve findings are visible in a screenshot a player would take: an English sentence standing in a German HUD, the same event logged twice in two languages, a warning about a ride that was repaired an hour ago, and a ride list showing one ride of four because the notification log beside it gets 442 px and the list gets 135. Also raw keys reaching the surface — a bare `thirst` and a bare `cores` — and temperatures in °C only. The critic notes five of the eight are between four lines and a two-word type change each, so round 2 is cheap.

rides.status: built, ungated — 4,879 lines in 10 files plus a 702-line selftest of 267 CHECKS, the largest in the project, wired as pnpm test:game-rides. THE FAIRGROUND TURNS. The cycle runs in the worker at 20 Hz in PARK MINUTES, so capacity / cycleMinutes x 60 is exact at every speed including the soak's 100x — measured, the carousel ran 19 cycles and 456 riders in one park hour against a rated 480. Loading is rate-limited rather than timed, so a quiet ride dispatches early. Breakdowns, downtime, service, queue with a wait estimate, throughput over a rolling park hour, utilisation, satisfaction. The animation is solved rather than eyeballed: two clocks (the cycle in park minutes, the machine in ride seconds) joined by a drive envelope; a chair swing's chains fly out at an angle solved from tan(theta) = omega^2 (r + L sin theta)/g, taking the seat radius 8.00 m -> 10.53 m at speed; ferris gondolas stay level and lag a degree on the ramps. Content: claims rideRigs, walks packs() AND onPack, switches on no id. Eleven parametric primitives; the showcase registers a runtime pack whose teacups are three levels of nested rotation, and the selftest registers a paratrooper in a third pack and asserts it is not a re-skin. In frame: 6 batches, 74 draw calls, 134 instances, 49,356 triangles = 6.2 % of the 1,200 budget. 0 console errors, 0 hydration warnings. The builder finished — the second of seven to survive to its own report. Six bugs were found by looking or by a check rather than by reading; the one worth repeating is that EVERY PRISM'S TOP CAP HAD ITS NORMAL POINTING DOWN, so every apron, platform and teacup floor rendered pure black, and it survived three rounds because a black slab on the ground reads as a shadow. Weak: guests have no hook yet (every rider so far came from rides:demo or an inspect()-scanning bridge; the eleven-line guests/sim.ts patch is requests/rides.md §1), no LOD, night is the weak hour with 3 lights on 6 machines, and the demo park's fairground plot is still empty — coordinates and yaws for five machines are in requests §6. GRADED round 1: 8.71, PASS — docs/game/critiques/rides-round1.md. The second module over the bar and, unlike track's 8.54, not sitting on it: two axes above 9 and none below 8.2. Strongest fidelity work in the project (a solved angle equation rather than a tuned one, and a throughput that arrives at its own arithmetic: 19 cycles and 456 riders in a park hour against a rated 480) and the strongest extensibility evidence anyone has produced (a runtime pack in the showcase, a THIRD pack in the selftest asserting a paratrooper is not a re-skin). openIssues: OPEN (environment, now measured across a whole day and the cause of a flat frame three other critiques blame): THE AUTO EXPOSURE CARRIES NO INFORMATION FROM 18:00 TO 06:00. Sampled on the environment showcase in clear weather: 05:00 3.6(MAX) · 06:00 3.6(MAX) · 07:00 2.825 · 08:00 2.327 · 10:00 2.012 · 12:00 1.954 · 14:00 2.012 · 16:00 2.327 · 17:30 3.557 · 18:00 3.6(MAX) · 18:30 3.6 · 19:00 3.6 · 19:30 3.6 · 20:00 3.6 · 21:00 3.6 · 22:00 3.6 · 00:00 3.6. Ten of seventeen sampled hours are pinned at EXPOSURE_MAX, and they include the whole golden and blue hour: at 18:00 the sun is still at intensity 0.392 and `night` is 0.02, and the camera is already at its ceiling. Dusk, twilight, full night and midnight are metered identically. The metering only ever moves 1.954 -> 3.557, i.e. 1.82x across the entire day, and it spends that whole range between noon and 17:30. Two things this does NOT say. The ceiling is not obviously wrong — an auto exposure that fully normalises a night scene makes night look like day, which is what EXPOSURE_MAX exists to prevent. And `contrast` sitting at 1.114 at every hour is by design: `mix(1.12, 0.98, env.cloud)` makes it a weather control rather than a time-of-day one. What is wrong is WHERE the curve reaches the ceiling. Between 17:30 and 18:30 the sun collapses 1.326 -> 0.392 -> 0.019, a 70x drop in an hour, so no exponent on the metering curve can hold dusk under the ceiling — the sun's own day curve is the thing to look at first, not the exposure's. Measured with .game-render/_probe/exposure-curve.mjs; NOT fixed, because tuning a day curve one SwiftShader frame at a time is how noon gets broken to fix dusk.

OPEN (core/renderer, D-027, and it was shipping to every Chrome and Edge visitor): THE WEBGPU PATH RENDERS A BLACK CANVAS. `game-shot.mjs` forces `?engine=webgl2` because headless Chromium has no WebGPU, so every frame in this project — every module grade, every critique, the whole gauntlet — was taken through the fallback, and nobody had looked at what a browser with `navigator.gpu` gets. It gets a black canvas with a working HUD over it: scene mounts, worker ticks, guests arrive, panels fill, 3D never drawn. Cause: the deep-import rule meets Babylon's shader store — `Materials/PBR/pbrMaterial` pulls `Shaders/pbr.vertex` (GLSL) and nothing pulls `ShadersWGSL/pbr.vertex`, so the engine has no shader for anything the game draws and the effect reads `shaderLanguage` off `undefined`: seven page errors before the first frame, `terrain` failing to start, repeated device loss. MITIGATED, NOT FIXED: WebGPU is opt-in now (`?engine=webgpu`) and the default is WebGL2, which demonstrably draws the park. The real fix is importing the WGSL twin of every shader the game uses (469 modules under `ShadersWGSL/`, PBR alone drags a long include list) and it is not done blind, because this container's WebGPU is SwiftShader and refuses the terrain's 7 MB vertex buffer whatever the shaders say — it needs somebody with a real GPU. `pnpm game:engine-probe` is the check: two Chromium launches, no engine query, mean luminance of the DRAWING BUFFER (not the screenshot — the HUD is opaque and would call a black park lit). Black is luma < 4; 13:00 measures 111, 23:00 measures in the twenties.

The sky, the fog and the exposure were all wrong in the same direction and are measured now. Three causes, each verified against a frame: (1) `scene.fogColor` was written as a LINEAR radiance, and Babylon runs `Color3.toLinearSpaceToRef` over it for every PBR material (`BindFogParameters`, `linearSpace` set), so the shader saw 0.034 where 0.295 was written — distant terrain got DARKER with distance instead of paler (sRGB 58/80/42 unfogged against 46/58/44 at 700 m). (2) The DOME painted `SkyState.ground` below the horizon, which is a term the IBL needs and the backdrop must not have: at the overview camera the terrain's far edge sits ~75 px under the true horizon and those 75 px were a dark olive band, sRGB 24/26/18 against the 75 the horizon ring rendered. That band is what several rounds of screenshots read as 'black above the horizon'.
